lead: This unit turns IoT ideas into working prototypes. You learn how Arduino and Raspberry Pi boards are set up, programmed and wired to sensors and actuators. After it, you can choose a board, read a sensor, drive an actuator and sketch a small IoT system end to end.
about: The unit moves from boards to a complete prototype. Chapter 4.1 covers Arduino boards, the IDE and the ecosystem. Chapter 4.2 adds Arduino C sketches, variables and digital I/O; only a few universities teach this at depth. Chapter 4.3 introduces the Raspberry Pi board, its interfaces and Linux. Chapter 4.4 programs the Pi in Python. Chapter 4.5 wires LEDs, push buttons, light, distance, temperature and humidity sensors to these boards and drives actuators. Chapter 4.6 compares other boards: ESP8266, BeagleBone and pcDuino. Chapter 4.7 pulls the parts into a simple IoT design with sensing, local decisions, wireless upload and action. Each chapter assumes the earlier one and points to protocol and cloud units rather than repeating them.

chapters.idea: An Arduino is a small open-source board that runs one program repeatedly and connects to physical pins through a simple IDE.
chapters.depth: Cover Arduino Uno, Nano and Mega at block level; the IDE steps: write, verify, upload; board package and libraries; shields and ecosystem; C++ basis. Some syllabi call the program a sketch and the language Arduino C/C++. Stay at pin names and setup/loop, not deep C++.

figure.title: From sketch to LED
figure.aria: Block diagram shows a sketch uploaded from a PC over USB to an Arduino, which drives an LED through a 1 kΩ resistor to ground.

chapters.example: An Arduino Uno runs at 5 V. An LED with forward voltage 2 V is connected to pin 9 through a 1 kΩ resistor. Find the current. Then give the loop that blinks it at 500 ms on and 500 ms off. Answer: I = (5 V − 2 V) ÷ 1000 Ω = 3 mA, where 5 V is the supply, 2 V is the LED forward voltage and 1000 Ω is the resistance. 3 mA is below the usual 20 mA pin limit. Use pinMode(9, OUTPUT); in setup, then digitalWrite(9, HIGH); delay(500); digitalWrite(9, LOW); delay(500); in loop.
chapters.trap: Do not connect a 5 V Arduino output straight to a 3.3 V sensor input; check per-pin current and use a resistor.
chapters.leave: Chapter 4.2 for sketches; Chapter 4.5 for sensor wiring; Unit 3 for communication.

chapters.idea: An Arduino sketch has two required functions, setup() and loop(), and uses typed variables and pin functions to read and write digital signals.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this as a separate programming chapter. Cover sketch structure, int/float/boolean, const, pinMode, digitalWrite, digitalRead, delay, if/else, serial print. Mention C++ syntax without classes. Keep to digital I/O; analogRead belongs later.

figure.title: Setup, loop and one button
figure.aria: Flowchart shows Arduino setup running once, then loop reading pin 2, testing HIGH and setting pin 13, then repeating.

chapters.example: A push button connects 5 V to Arduino pin 2. A 10 kΩ resistor pulls pin 2 to ground. An LED is on pin 13. Write the setup and loop so the LED is on only while the button is pressed. Find the pull-down current when pressed. Answer: pinMode(2, INPUT); pinMode(13, OUTPUT);. In loop, if digitalRead(2) is HIGH, set pin 13 HIGH; else set it LOW. Pull-down current = 5 V ÷ 10 kΩ = 0.5 mA, where 5 V is the pressed pin voltage and 10 kΩ is the resistor.
chapters.trap: INPUT_PULLUP inverts logic: with a pull-up, a pressed button to ground reads LOW.
chapters.leave: Analog sensors to Chapter 4.5; serial protocols to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: A Raspberry Pi is a small single-board computer that runs Linux, so it has a full OS, file system and 3.3 V GPIO header.
chapters.depth: Cover board blocks: SoC, RAM, microSD, USB, Ethernet/Wi-Fi, HDMI, 40-pin GPIO; 3.3 V logic; interfaces UART, I2C, SPI, PWM; Linux boot, user account, terminal, apt, files. Some syllabi say Raspberry Pi OS, formerly Raspbian. Avoid deep kernel.

figure.aria: Stack diagram shows application and Python above Linux libraries and kernel, ending at the 3.3 V GPIO header.

chapters.example: A red LED with forward voltage 2.0 V is driven from a Raspberry Pi GPIO at 3.3 V. The design target is 5 mA. Find the series resistor and the nearest standard value. Answer: R = (3.3 V − 2.0 V) ÷ 0.005 A = 260 Ω, where 3.3 V is the GPIO high voltage, 2.0 V is the LED forward voltage and 0.005 A is 5 mA. Use 270 Ω; the current becomes (3.3 V − 2.0 V) ÷ 270 Ω = 4.81 mA.
chapters.trap: Raspberry Pi GPIO is 3.3 V and not 5 V tolerant; a 5 V sensor output can damage it.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2: single-board computers; basic Linux helpful.
chapters.leave: Python to Chapter 4.4; sensor details to Chapter 4.5.

chapters.idea: Python on the Raspberry Pi reads and writes GPIO pins through libraries, so control logic is short and readable.
chapters.depth: Cover variables, lists, loops, functions, if, importing modules, running a script; gpiozero LED/Button; RPi.GPIO names; time.sleep; reading an ADC over SPI for analog sensors. Note the Pi has no analog input.

figure.aria: Sequence diagram shows a Python script asking gpiozero, MCP3008 and LM35 for a reading, returning raw 62 and 20.0 °C.

chapters.example: An LM35 sensor outputs 10 mV per °C. It feeds channel 0 of an MCP3008 10-bit ADC with reference 3.3 V. Python reads raw value 62. Find the ADC input voltage and the temperature. Answer: V = 62 ÷ 1023 × 3.3 V = 0.200 V, where 62 is the raw ADC code, 1023 is the 10-bit full scale and 3.3 V is the reference. T = 0.200 V ÷ 0.010 V/°C = 20.0 °C, where 0.010 V/°C is the LM35 sensitivity.
chapters.trap: Forgetting that the Pi has no analog pins and trying analogRead(); use an external ADC such as MCP3008 or ADS1115.
chapters.leave: Sensor physics to Chapter 4.5; cloud upload to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Sensors turn a physical quantity into a voltage or digital signal, and the board turns that reading into an actuator action.
chapters.depth: Cover LEDs and push buttons as basic I/O; LDR light intensity with a voltage divider; HC-SR04 ultrasonic timing; LM35 temperature; DHT11/DHT22 humidity; relay, buzzer and motor driver as actuators. Show sensor-actuator interaction with a threshold. Mention 3.3 V versus 5 V level shifting.

figure.title: Ultrasonic sensor to buzzer
figure.aria: Block diagram shows an Arduino triggering HC-SR04, timing the echo, computing distance and sounding a buzzer below 20 cm.

chapters.example: An HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor sends a trigger pulse. The echo pulse stays high for 580 µs. Take speed of sound as 343 m/s. Find the distance to the object. Answer: d = v × t ÷ 2 = 343 m/s × 580 × 10⁻⁶ s ÷ 2 = 0.09947 m = 9.95 cm, where d is distance, v is speed of sound, t is echo pulse time and the division by 2 removes the round trip.
chapters.trap: Using the full echo time as one-way distance doubles the answer; divide by 2. Also convert µs to s.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4.2 digital I/O; Chapter 4.3 GPIO; basic voltage divider.
chapters.leave: Communication protocols to Unit 3; sensor types to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: ESP8266, BeagleBone and pcDuino fill different gaps: Wi-Fi only, Linux with real-time I/O, and Arduino-like Linux boards.
chapters.depth: Compare ESP8266 NodeMCU (3.3 V, Wi-Fi, Arduino IDE), BeagleBone Black (Linux, many GPIO, PRUs), pcDuino (Arduino headers plus Linux). Mention Cubieboard only as another name some syllabi use. Keep to selection criteria: voltage, OS, wireless, pins, power.

figure.aria: Tree diagram groups Arduino, Raspberry Pi, ESP8266, BeagleBone and pcDuino under IoT boards.

chapters.example: An ESP8266 NodeMCU draws 80 mA while awake for 2 s and 20 µA in deep sleep for 58 s in every 60 s cycle. Find the average current. Answer: convert 20 µA = 0.020 mA. Average = (80 mA × 2 s + 0.020 mA × 58 s) ÷ 60 s = (160 + 1.16) ÷ 60 = 2.686 mA ≈ 2.69 mA, where 80 mA is the awake current, 2 s is the awake time, 0.020 mA is the sleep current and 60 s is the cycle.
chapters.trap: ESP8266 and ESP32 GPIO are 3.3 V and not 5 V tolerant; a 5 V sensor output needs a divider or level shifter.
chapters.leave: Protocol details to Unit 3; cloud to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: A simple IoT system repeats four steps: sense, decide, act and report, with a safe fallback when the network fails.
chapters.depth: Cover design flow: define goal and thresholds; choose board and sensor; local control loop; wireless module; MQTT topic or HTTP endpoint; dashboard; power and enclosure; fail-safe. Use a home water tank example. Mention security at high level and point to Unit 5.

figure.title: Water tank IoT loop
figure.aria: Block diagram shows an ultrasonic sensor feeding an ESP8266 that starts a pump through a relay at low level and publishes readings to an MQTT cloud dashboard.

chapters.example: A home water tank is 100 cm tall with base area 1 m². An ultrasonic sensor at the top reads distance d = 70 cm to the water. Find water height and volume. The pump starts at level ≤ 30 cm and stops at level ≥ 90 cm. State the action at d = 70 cm. Answer: height = 100 cm − 70 cm = 30 cm, where 100 cm is tank height and 70 cm is the empty space. Base area 1 m² = 10,000 cm². Volume = 30 cm × 10,000 cm² = 300,000 cm³ = 300 L. At exactly 30 cm, if the rule is ≤, the pump starts; write the rule exactly to avoid chattering.
chapters.trap: The sensor measures empty space from the top, not water depth; subtract from tank height. Add hysteresis so the relay does not chatter at the threshold.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 4.5 and 4.6; Unit 3 MQTT basics; Unit 5 cloud.
chapters.leave: Cloud platform details to Unit 5; security design to Unit 5.
